1.o: This chapter gives us a particular account what sort of progress the several tribes of Israel made in the reducing of Canaan after the death of Joshua. He did (as we say) break the neck of that great work, and put it into such a posture that they might easily have perfected it in due time, if they had not been wanting to themselves; what they did in order hereunto, and wherein they came short, we are told. I. The united tribes of Judah and Simeon did bravely. 1. God appointed Judah to begin, ver. 1, 2. 2.
1.i: Acsah asks her father Caleb for springs of water, and her husband Othniel becomes Israel's first judge.
1.p: Lord, You give water in dry lands. Raise up faithful people to lead us, and teach us to ask boldly. Amen.
1.l: Ask boldly for something good for your family today, and then thank the person who gives it.
q: Acsah asked for springs, and Caleb gave her more. What good thing do you need to ask for?

2.o: In this chapter we have, I. A particular message which God sent to Israel by an angel, and the impression it made upon them, ver. 1-5. II. A general idea of the state of Israel during the government of the judges, in which observe, 1. Their adherence to God while Joshua and the elders lived, ver. 6-10. 2. Their revolt afterwards to idolatry, ver. 11-13. 3. God's displeasure against them, and his judgments upon them for it, ver. 14, 15. 4. His pity towards them, shown in raising them up deliverers, ver. 16-18. 5.
2.i: Judges 2 is the preface to the whole book: a warning, a funeral, and a pattern that repeats.
2.p: Lord, You never forget Your people. Help us to remember what You have done, and to teach it to the next generation. Amen.
2.l: Ask an older person in your family to tell you one thing God has done for them, so that you do not forget.
q: The next generation had not been taught. What are you teaching deliberately and what are you assuming they'll pick up?

3.o: In this chapter, I. A general account of Israel's enemies is premised, and of the mischief they did them, ver. 1-7. II. A particular account of the brave exploits done by the first three of the judges. 1. Othniel, whom God raised up to fight Israel's battles, and plead their cause against the king of Mesopotamia, ver. 8-11. 2. Ehud, who was employed in rescuing Israel out of the hands of the Moabites, and did it by stabbing the king of Moab, ver. 12-30. 3.
3.i: Acsah asks her father Caleb for springs of water, and her husband Othniel becomes Israel's first judge.
3.p: Lord, You give water in dry lands. Raise up faithful people to lead us, and teach us to ask boldly. Amen.
3.l: Ask boldly for something good for your family today, and then thank the person who gives it.
q: Acsah asked for springs, and Caleb gave her more. What good thing do you need to ask for?

4.o: The method of the history of Deborah and Barak (the heroes in this chapter) is the same with that before. Here is, I. Israel revolted from God, ver. 1. II. Israel oppressed by Jabin, ver. 2, 3. III. Israel judged by Deborah, ver. 4, 5. IV. Israel rescued out of the hands of Jabin. 1. Their deliverance is concerted between Deborah and Barak, ver. 6, 9. 2. It is accomplished by their joint-agency. Barak takes the field, ver. 10. Sisera, Jabin's general, meets him, ver. 12, 13. Deborah encourages him, ver. 14.
4.i: Deborah, a judge and prophetess, called Barak to lead Israel against Sisera's iron chariots, and God gave them a victory at the river Kishon.
4.p: Lord, thank You for leaders like Deborah. Make us brave to follow when You call. Amen.
4.l: Be brave like Barak. If God has asked you to do something hard, say yes, and take a friend who encourages you.
q: Barak said he would go only if Deborah went too. Who helps you be brave?

5.o: This chapter contains the triumphal song which was composed and sung upon occasion of that glorious victory which Israel obtained over the forces of Jabin king of Canaan and the happy consequences of that victory. Probably it was usual then to publish poems upon such occasions, as now; but this only is preserved of all the poems of that age of the judges, because dictated by Deborah a prophetess, designed for a psalm of praise then, and a pattern of praise to after-ages, and it gives a great deal of light to the…
5.i: Sisera fled to Jael's tent and was defeated there, and Deborah and Barak sang a victory song that credited the Lord with Israel's freedom.
5.p: Lord, we thank You for those who stand up for Your people. May Your friends shine like the sun. Amen.
5.l: Today, say thank you to someone brave who has stood up for others.
q: Deborah's song gave the credit to the Lord. Whom do you thank when a hard thing turns out well?

6.o: Nothing that occurred in the quiet and peaceable times of Israel is recorded; the forty years' rest after the conquest of Jabin is passed over in silence; and here begins the story of another distress and another deliverance, by Gideon, the fourth of the judges. Here is, I. The calamitous condition of Israel, by the inroads of the Midianites, ver. 1-6. II. The message God sent them by a prophet, by convincing them of sin, to prepare them for deliverance, ver. 7-10. III.
6.s: The Mighty Man Hiding in the Winepress
6.i: An angel found Gideon hiding in a winepress and called him a mighty warrior, promising that God would be with him as he saved Israel.
6.p: Lord, You call us by what we will become. Give us courage, as You gave Gideon, to answer when You send us. Amen.
6.l: Say out loud one good thing God might see in you that you do not see in yourself.
q: God called Gideon a mighty warrior while he was hiding. What might God see in you that you cannot see yet?

7.o: This chapter presents us with Gideon in the field, commanding the army of Israel, and routing the army of the Midianites, for which great exploit we found in the former chapter how he was prepared by his converse with God and his conquest of Baal. We are here told, I. What direction God gave to Gideon for the modelling of his army, by which it was reduced to 300 men, ver. 1, 8. II.
7.i: Gideon's three hundred surrounded the Midianite camp at midnight with trumpets, jars and torches, and God turned the enemy against itself.
7.p: Lord, make us willing to do small things in Your way, and to give You the glory. Amen.
7.l: Do something brave but quiet today: help someone, and let God get the credit.
q: The jars were everyday water pitchers carried by women. What ordinary tool in your hands could do more than you expect?

8.o: This chapter gives us a further account of Gideon's victory over the Midianites, with the residue of the story of his life and government. I. Gideon prudently pacifies the offended Ephraimites, ver. 1-3. II. He bravely pursues the flying Midianites, ver. 4, 10-12. III. He justly chastises the insolence of the men of Succoth and Penuel, who basely abused him (ver. 5-9), and were reckoned with for it, ver. 13-17. IV. He honourably slays the two kings of Midian, ver. 18-21. V.
8.i: Judges 8 shows a hero turning down a crown, and then making a mistake that trips up his own family.
8.p: Lord, You are our only King. Keep us from making good things into idols, and keep us loyal to You after our heroes are gone. Amen.
8.l: Ask yourself today what you might be treating as more important than God, even a good thing.
q: Gideon's good intention still led to a sin. What good intention of yours has quietly become a snare?

9.o: The apostasy of Israel after the death of Gideon is punished, not as the former apostasies by a foreign invasion, or the oppressions of any neighbouring power, but by intestine broils among themselves, which in this chapter we have the story of; and it is hard to say whether their sin or their misery appears most in it. It is an account of the usurpation and tyranny of Abimelech, who was base son to Gideon; so we must call him, and not more modishly his natural son: he was so unlike him. We are here told, I.
9.i: After Abimelech murdered his brothers and became king, Jotham told a fable from Mount Gerizim: the good trees would not rule, but the thornbush would.
9.p: Lord, give us leaders who serve and not just rule, and make us servants ourselves. Amen.
9.l: Think about the people you admire. Are they busy doing good, or just hungry for power? Choose to follow good leaders.
q: The good trees would not leave their fruit to rule. What good work are you unwilling to leave for status?

10.o: In this chapter we have, I. The peaceable times Israel enjoyed under the government of two judges, Tola and Jair, ver. 1-5. II. The troublesome times that ensued. 1. Israel's sin that brought them into trouble, ver. 6. 2. The trouble itself they were in, ver. 7-9. III. Their repentance and humiliation for sin, their prayers and reformation, and the mercy they found with God thereupon, ver. 10-16. IV. Preparation made for their deliverance out of the hand of their oppressors, ver. 17, 18.
10.i: Judges 10 and 12 begin with a nation in trouble because of its idols, and end with a civil war over hurt pride.
10.p: Lord, You are patient with our failures. Help us to turn from idols, and to settle our quarrels before they become wars. Amen.
10.l: Choose today to settle a quarrel with words, before it grows into something worse.
q: Any word with that sound would have worked as a test. What small, arbitrary mark do you use to decide who belongs?

11.o: This chapter gives as the history of Jephthah, another of Israel's judges, and numbered among the worthies of the Old Testament, that by faith did great things (Heb. xi. 32), though he had not such an extraordinary call as the rest there mentioned had. Here we have, I. The disadvantages of his origin, ver. 1-3. II. The Gileadites' choice of him to be commander-in-chief against the Ammonites, and the terms he made with them, ver. 4-11. III.
11.i: The elders of Gilead, who had driven Jephthah out, came to him in their trouble and asked him to lead them, and he agreed.
11.p: Lord, You call the rejected and the overlooked. Teach us to welcome those we have pushed away. Amen.
11.l: Think about someone who gets left out at your school or church. Invite them to join you today.
q: The people who rejected Jephthah needed him. Who have you pushed aside who might be exactly who you need?

12.o: In this chapter we have, I. Jephthah's rencounter with the Ephraimites, and the blood shed on that unhappy occasion (ver. 1-6), and the conclusion of Jephthah's life and government, ver. 7. II. A short account of three other of the judges of Israel: Ibzan (ver. 8-10), Elon (ver. 11, 12), Abdon, ver. 13-15.
12.i: Judges 10 and 12 begin with a nation in trouble because of its idols, and end with a civil war over hurt pride.
12.p: Lord, You are patient with our failures. Help us to turn from idols, and to settle our quarrels before they become wars. Amen.
12.l: Choose today to settle a quarrel with words, before it grows into something worse.
q: Any word with that sound would have worked as a test. What small, arbitrary mark do you use to decide who belongs?

13.o: At this chapter begins the story of Samson, the last of the judges of Israel whose story is recorded in this book, and next before Eli. The passages related concerning him are, from first to last, very surprising and uncommon. The figure he makes in this history is really great, and yet vastly different from that of his predecessors.
13.i: An angel promised a childless couple in Zorah that they would have a son, Samson, who would be set apart to God and begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
13.p: Lord, You answer the prayers of the childless and the lonely. Raise up children for You, and give parents wisdom. Amen.
13.l: Tell someone today how God has answered one of your prayers. Share your joy with them.
q: Manoah's wife reasoned from God's actions to His purpose. What might God's past goodness be telling you now?

14.o: The idea which this chapter gives us of Samson is not what one might have expected concerning one who, by the special designation of heaven, was a Nazarite to God and a deliverer of Israel; and yet really he was both. Here is, I. Samson's courtship of a daughter of the Philistines, and his marriage to her, ver. 1-5, 7, 8. II. His conquest of a lion, and the prize he found in the carcase of it, ver. 5, 6, 8, 9. III. Samson's riddle proposed to his companions (ver.
14.i: Samson tells a riddle at his wedding feast, and the Philistines get the answer from his wife.
14.p: Lord, You use even our mistakes. Give us wisdom to choose well and to keep our promises. Amen.
14.l: Make up a riddle for a friend today, and ask them to guess.
q: Samson shared a secret and it was used against him. How do you decide what to share and with whom?

15.o: Samson, when he courted an alliance with the Philistines, did but seek an occasion against them, ch. xiv. 4. Now here we have a further account of the occasions he took to weaken them, and to avenge, not his own, but Israel's quarrels, upon them.
15.i: At Lehi, Samson broke free of his bonds, defeated a Philistine force with a jawbone, and cried to God for water, and God opened a spring.
15.p: Lord, You give strength and You give water. Teach us to depend on You, even when we feel strong. Amen.
15.l: When you are very tired or thirsty, tell God, like Samson did. And drink a glass of water slowly, and thank Him.
q: Samson was a strong man who still needed to ask for water. What do you need to ask God for, even if you are strong?

16.o: Samson's name (we have observed before) signifies a little sun (sol parvus); we have seen this sun rising very bright, and his morning ray strong and clear; and, nothing appearing to the contrary, we take it for granted that the middle of the day was proportionably illustrious, while he judged Israel twenty years; but the melancholy story of this chapter gives us such an account of his evening as did not commend his day.
16.i: Judges 16 tells how Israel's strongest judge lost his strength, not through a stronger enemy, but through his own carelessness.
16.p: Lord, You gave Samson his strength, and You are the source of ours. Keep us from carelessness, and bring us back when we fail. Amen.
16.l: Think today about who you tell your most important secrets to, and whether they have earned your trust.
q: The text says the Lord had left him and he did not know it. What might you be depending on that has already gone?

17.o: All agree that what is related in this and the rest of the chapters to the end of this book was not done, as the narrative occurs, after Samson, but long before, even soon after the death of Joshua, in the days of Phinehas the son of Eleazar, ch. xx. 28. But it is cast here into the latter part of the book that it might not interrupt the history of the Judges. That it might appear how happy the nation was in the judges it is here shown how unhappy they were when there was none. I.
17.i: Judges 17 begins the book's two-chapter appendix, and shows how far religion had drifted from God's commands in the days before kings.
17.p: Lord, keep us from making our own religion. Show us Your ways, and help us to walk in them. Amen.
17.l: Check one habit today against what God says, not only against what feels right.
q: Micah thought himself holier than his neighbors. Where do you assume your religion makes you safe?

18.o: How idolatry crept into the family of Micah we read in the preceding chapter, how it was translated thence into the tribe of Dan we have an account in this chapter, and how it gained a settlement in a city of note; for how great a matter does a little fire kindle! The tribe of Dan had their lot assigned them last of all the tribes, and, it happening to be too strait for them, a considerable city in the utmost corner of Canaan northward was added to it. "Let them get it, and take it;"
18.i: The tribe of Dan, short of land, took a quiet city in the far north, renamed it Dan, and brought with them an idol and a wandering priest.
18.p: Lord, keep us from taking what is not ours. Make us people who seek Your way. Amen.
18.l: Think about a time you took something that was not yours. Tell someone, and make it right.
q: The Danites did what was right in their own eyes. How do you decide what is right?

19.o: The three remaining chapters of this book contain a most tragical story of the wickedness of the men of Gibeah, patronised by the tribe of Benjamin, for which that tribe was severely chastised and almost entirely cut off by the rest of the tribes. This seems to have been done not long after the death of Joshua, for it was when there was no king, no judge, in Israel (ver. 1, and ch. xxi. 25), and Phinehas was then high priest, ch. xx. 28.
19.i: Judges 19 to 21 is the Bible's darkest chapter set, and it is placed last in the book to show where doing what is right in your own eyes leads.
19.p: Lord, we see how far people go without You. Be our King, and heal the places where right and wrong have been forgotten. Amen.
19.l: Ask a grown-up to read the end of Judges with you, and talk about why Israel needed a king who followed God.
q: Disorder shows first where there is no government. What small rules at home or work keep trouble from growing?

20.o: Into the book of the wars of the Lord the story of this chapter must be brought, but it looks as sad and uncomfortable as any article in all that history; for there is nothing in it that looks in the least bright or pleasant but the pious zeal of Israel against the wickedness of the men of Gibeah, which made it on their side a just and holy war; but otherwise the obstinacy of the Benjamites in protecting their criminals, which was the foundation of the war, the vast loss which the Israelites sustained in carrying…
20.i: Judges 19 to 21 is the Bible's darkest chapter set, and it is placed last in the book to show where doing what is right in your own eyes leads.
20.p: Lord, we see how far people go without You. Be our King, and heal the places where right and wrong have been forgotten. Amen.
20.l: Ask a grown-up to read the end of Judges with you, and talk about why Israel needed a king who followed God.
q: Disorder shows first where there is no government. What small rules at home or work keep trouble from growing?

21.o: The ruins of the tribe of Benjamin we read of in the foregoing chapter; now here we have, I. The lamentation which Israel made over these ruins, ver. 1-4, 6, 15. II. The provision they made for the repair of them out of the 600 men that escaped, for whom they procured wives, 1. Of the virgins of Jabesh-Gilead, when they destroyed that city for not sending its forces to the general rendezvous, ver. 5, 7-14. 2. Of the daughters of Shiloh, ver. 16-25. And so this melancholy story concludes.
21.i: Judges 19 to 21 is the Bible's darkest chapter set, and it is placed last in the book to show where doing what is right in your own eyes leads.
21.p: Lord, we see how far people go without You. Be our King, and heal the places where right and wrong have been forgotten. Amen.
21.l: Ask a grown-up to read the end of Judges with you, and talk about why Israel needed a king who followed God.
q: Disorder shows first where there is no government. What small rules at home or work keep trouble from growing?
